summary: This paper addresses the problem of mapping program qubits to logical qubits in high-rate quantum error detection codes, specifically the $[[4,2,2]]$ Iceberg code which encodes two logical qubits per patch. The authors present a compilation framework combining Hadamard commutation, gate merging, and noise-biased packing heuristics that reduces circuit depth by 34%, gate counts by 31% and 17% for one- and two-qubit gates respectively, and improves logical selection rate by 86% relative to naive compilation.
motivation: Current quantum error detecting/correcting architectures require high-rate codes with $k > 1$ logical qubits per patch due to limited physical qubit counts, but the optimal assignment of program qubits to these patches has not been previously studied, creating a critical gap in compilation techniques as codes with multiple logical qubits reduce error tolerance and make qubit placement decisions material to circuit fidelity.
method: The framework performs Hadamard commutation to reduce expensive single-qubit gates, executes gate merging to combine compatible operations into cheaper transversal or patch-wise implementations, and employs a greedy packing heuristic with noise-biased scoring (weighting merge savings, delay penalties, and gate-type preferences) to solve the qubit assignment problem in $O(n^2 \cdot m \log m)$ time, avoiding the $O(n!)$ brute-force search.
result: Across 71 QASMBench circuits up to 150 logical qubits, the framework achieves average reductions of 31% in single-qubit gates, 17% in two-qubit gates, 34% in depth, improves total variation distance by 1.75$\times$, and logical selection rate by 86%, with gains remaining stable as circuits scale and greatest improvements at tight packing density ($n/k = 2$).
